arXiv:1609.04676v1 [math.AG] 15 Sep 2016

Localization, local cohomology, and the bb-function
of a DD-module with respect to a polynomial

Toshinori Oaku
Abstract

Given a DD-module MM generated by a single element, and a polynomial ff, one can construct several DD-modules attached to MM and ff and can define the notion of the (generalized) bb-function following M. Kashiwara. These modules are closely related to the localization and the local cohomology of MM. We show that the bb-function, if it exists, controls these modules and present general algorithms for computing these modules and the bb-function (if it exists) without any further assumptions. We also give some examples of multiplicity computation of such DD-modules

Introduction

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x]=K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be the polynomial ring in nn variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). Let Dn=K[x]⟨∂⟩=K[x]⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩D_{n}=K[x]\langle\partial\rangle=K[x]\langle\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\rangle be the nn-th Weyl algebra, i.e., the ring of differential operators with polynomial coefficients with respect to the variables xx, where we denote ∂=(∂1,…,∂x)\partial=(\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{x}) with ∂i=∂xi=∂/∂xi\partial_{i}=\partial_{x_{i}}=\partial/\partial x_{i} being the derivation with respect to xix_{i}. An arbitrary element PP of DnD_{n} is written in a finite sum

P=∑α∈ℕnaα(x)∂αwithaα(x)∈K[x],P=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{\alpha}(x)\partial^{\alpha}\quad\mbox{with}\quad a_{\alpha}(x)\in K[x],

where we denote ∂α=∂1α1⋯∂nαn\partial^{\alpha}=\partial_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\partial_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} for a multi-index α=(α1,…,αn)∈ℕn\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with ℕ{\mathbb{N}} being the set of non-negative integers. One can define the dimension of a finitely generated left DXD_{X}-module MM; J. Bernstein [1], [2] proved that the dimension of MM is not less than nn unless MM is the zero module. A finitely generated left DnD_{n}-module is called holonomic if its dimension is nn or else it is the zero module.

Let MM be a finitely generated left DnD_{n}-module and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] be a non-constant polynomial. Then the localization M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] and the local cohomology groups H(f)j​(M)H^{j}_{(f)}(M) have natural structures of left DnD_{n}-module and are holonomic if so is MM, as was shown by Kashiwara [7]. More generally, one can construct a left Dn​[s]D_{n}[s]-module M⁡(u,f,s)=Dn​[s]​(u⊗fs)M(u,f,s)=D_{n}[s](u\otimes f^{s}) with an indeterminate ss. Suppose that MM is generated by uu over DnD_{n}. Then the (generalized) bb-function for uu and ff is defined to be the univariate (and monic) polynomial bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) of the least degree such that

bu,f​(s)​(u⊗fs)∈Dn​[s]​(u⊗fs+1)b_{u,f}(s)(u\otimes f^{s})\in D_{n}[s](u\otimes f^{s+1})

holds. The existence of bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) was proved by Kashiwara [7] under the assumption that MM is holonomic outside of the hypersurface f=0f=0. If MM is the polynomial ring K⁡[x]K[x] with u=1u=1, then bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) is nothing but the classical Bernstein-Sato polynomial, or simply the bb-function, of ff. In the same way as the Bernstein-Sato polynomial controls the localization of the polynomial ring as a DnD_{n}-module, the bb-function controls the localization M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] or its generalization Dn​(u⊗fλ)D_{n}(u\otimes f^{\lambda}).

On the other hand, algorithms to compute M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) and the bb-function if it exists were introduced in [10] under the assumption that MM is ff-torsion free. These algorithms are based on various Gröbner bases over the ring of differential operators as is presented, e.g., in [15] and [11]. Torrelli [16] studied the bb-function bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) systematically when MM is the local cohomology group H(f1,…,fk)k​(K⁡[x])H^{k}_{(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})}(K[x]) under the assumption that f1,…,fk,ff_{1},\dots,f_{k},f define a quasi-homogeneous non-isolated singularity, together with the general property of M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) under the assumption that MM is holonomic without ff-torsion.

The purpose of our study on the bb-function and M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) is twofold: first, we want to clarify how the bb-function controls the module M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) and the localization M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] as well as the local cohomology H(f)1​(M)H^{1}_{(f)}(M). This will be performed in Sections 1 and 4. These results should be more or less well-known under some stronger conditions. See, e.g., [16] and Chapter VI of [3], where MM is assumed to be ff-torsion free, or regular holonomic. The second purpose is to remove the assumption of ff-saturatedness from our former algorithms in [10]. For this purpose, we reinterpret the algorithm introduced in [14] for the localization M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] in Section 2. Our algorithms work at least if MM is holonomic outside of f=0f=0 without any further assumptions.

In the last section, we study the multiplicity (in the sense of Bernstein [1]) and the length of a holonomic DD-module, as the most fundamental numerical invariants. This can be also used to prove a relation between bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) and M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda). We also give some examples of the multiplicity computation of the localization or the local cohomology.

We use computer algebra system Risa/Asir [9] for computation of Gröbner bases over the ring of differential operators, and in particular, for computation of DD-module theoretic integration, which is needed in the localization algorithm.

1 The bb-function for a DD-module and a polynomial after Kashiwara

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and X=KnX=K^{n} be the nn-dimensional affine space over KK. We denote by DXD_{X} the nn-th Weyl algebra DnD_{n} over KK. Let MM be a left DXD_{X}-module and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] a non-constant polynomial. We can associate several DXD_{X}-modules with MM and ff by translating the definitions by Kashiwara [7] for analytic DD-modules to algebraic setting. First, the localization M⁡[f−1]:=M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]M[f^{-1}]:=M\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}] and the local cohomology groups H(f)j​(M)H^{j}_{(f)}(M) (j=0,1j=0,1) are defined with MM being regarded as a K⁡[x]K[x]-module; they become again left DXD_{X}-modules.

Introducing an indeterminate ss, let

ℒ:=K⁡[x,f−1,s]​fs{\mathcal{L}}:=K[x,f^{-1},s]f^{s}

be the free K⁡[x,f−1,s]K[x,f^{-1},s]-module with a free generator fsf^{s}. Then ℒ{\mathcal{L}} has a natural structure of left DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-module through the action of xix_{i} on ℒ{\mathcal{L}} defined by

∂xi(a⁡(x,s)​f−k​fs)=(∂a⁡(x,s)∂xi​f−k+(s−k)​fi​a​(x,s)​f−k−1)​fs(1≤i≤n)\partial_{x_{i}}(a(x,s)f^{-k}f^{s})=\left(\frac{\partial a(x,s)}{\partial x_{i}}f^{-k}+(s-k)f_{i}a(x,s)f^{-k-1}\right)f^{s}\qquad(1\leq i\leq n)

with fi:=∂f/∂xif_{i}:=\partial f/\partial x_{i}. Sometimes f−k​fsf^{-k}f^{s} is abbreviated to fs−kf^{s-k}.

The tensor product M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}} has a natural structure of left DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-module induced by

∂xi(u⊗a⁡(x,s)​fs)=(∂xiu)⊗a⁡(x,s)​fs+u⊗∂xi(a⁡(x,s)​fs)(1≤i≤n)\partial_{x_{i}}(u\otimes a(x,s)f^{s})=(\partial_{x_{i}}u)\otimes a(x,s)f^{s}+u\otimes\partial_{x_{i}}(a(x,s)f^{s})\quad(1\leq i\leq n)

for u∈Mu\in M and a⁡(x,s)∈K⁡[x,s]a(x,s)\in K[x,s]. In what follows, we fix an arbitrary nonzero element uu of MM. Let M⁡(u,f,s):=DX​[s]​(u⊗fs)M(u,f,s):=D_{X}[s](u\otimes f^{s}) be the left DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-submodule of M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}} generated by u⊗fsu\otimes f^{s}. Set

I⁡(u,f):={b⁡(s)∈K⁡[x]∣b⁡(s)​(u⊗fs)=P⁡(s)​(f​u⊗fs)=0​ for some P⁡(s)∈DX}.I(u,f):=\{b(s)\in K[x]\mid b(s)(u\otimes f^{s})=P(s)(fu\otimes f^{s})=0\mbox{ for some $P(s)\in D_{X}$}\}.

If I⁡(u,f)≠{0}I(u,f)\neq\{0\}, then the (monic) generator bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) of I⁡(u,f)I(u,f) is called the (generalized) bb-function for uu and ff. It was defined by Kashiwara [7] with the following existence theorem.

Theorem 1.1 (Kashiwara [7])

If MM is holonomic on Xf={x∈X∣f⁡(x)≠0}X_{f}=\{x\in X\mid f(x)\neq 0\}, then I⁡(u,f)≠{0}I(u,f)\neq\{0\}.

When M=K⁡[x]M=K[x] and u=1u=1, the bb-function b1,f​(s)b_{1,f}(s) is nothing but what is called the Bernstein-Sato polynomial, or the bb-function, associated with ff. In fact, Kashiwara proved this theorem for a module MM over the ring of differential operators with analytic coefficients and a complex analytic function ff. This corresponds to what is called the local bb-function. The coincidence of the local bb-functions in the algebraic setting and in the analytic setting is noticed, e.g., as Corollary 8.6 of [10]. It will turn out in what follows that the bb-function ‘controls’ the DD-modules associated with MM and ff.

The bb-function can exist even if MM is not holonomic on XfX_{f}.

Example 1.2

Set n=2n=2, x1=xx_{1}=x, x2=yx_{2}=y, and P=x∂x2+∂yP=x\partial_{x}^{2}+\partial_{y}. Then M:=DX/DX​P=DX​uM:=D_{X}/D_{X}P=D_{X}u with uu being the residue class of 11 is not holonomic even outside of x=0x=0 (the dimension of MM is three), but has the bb-functions bu,x​(s)=(s+1)​(s+2)b_{u,x}(s)=(s+1)(s+2) and bu,y​(s)=s+1b_{u,y}(s)=s+1. In fact, one has

(−x∂x2+2(s+1)∂x−∂y)(u⊗xs+1)=(s+1)(s+2)u⊗xs,P(u⊗ys+1)=(s+1)u⊗ys(-x\partial_{x}^{2}+2(s+1)\partial_{x}-\partial_{y})(u\otimes x^{s+1})=(s+1)(s+2)u\otimes x^{s},\qquad P(u\otimes y^{s+1})=(s+1)u\otimes y^{s}

in M⊗K⁡[x,y]K⁡[x,y,x−1]​xsM\otimes_{K[x,y]}K[x,y,x^{-1}]x^{s} and in M⊗K⁡[x,y]K⁡[x,y,y−1]​ysM\otimes_{K[x,y]}K[x,y,y^{-1}]y^{s} respectively.

An algorithm to determine if there exists the bb-function and to compute it if it exists was given in [10] under the assumption that M=DX​uM=D_{X}u is ff-torsion free, or ff-saturated, i.e., the homomorphism f:M→Mf:M\rightarrow M is injective.

Let us define a DXD_{X}-automorphism t:ℒ→ℒt:{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{L}} by

t⁡(a⁡(x,s)​f−k​fs)=a⁡(x,s+1)​f−k+1​fst(a(x,s)f^{-k}f^{s})=a(x,s+1)f^{-k+1}f^{s}

for a⁡(x,s)∈K⁡[x,s]a(x,s)\in K[x,s] and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. The inverse t−1t^{-1} is defined by

t−1​(a⁡(x,s)​f−k​fs)=a⁡(x,s−1)​f−k−1​fs.t^{-1}(a(x,s)f^{-k}f^{s})=a(x,s-1)f^{-k-1}f^{s}.

It induces a DXD_{X}-automorphism

t:M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ⟶M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ,t:M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}\longrightarrow M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}},

which also induces a DXD_{X}-endomorphism of M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s).　 Note that the actions of tt and ss on M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) satisfies the commutation relation s​t=t⁡(s−1)st=t(s-1). It follows that t​M​(u,f,s)tM(u,f,s) is a left DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-module. It also follows from the definition that bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) is the minimal polynomial of the action ss on the left DXD_{X}-module M⁡(u,f,s)/t​M​(u,f,s)M(u,f,s)/tM(u,f,s) since P⁡(s)​(f​u⊗fs)=t⁡(P⁡(s−1)​(u⊗fs))P(s)(fu\otimes f^{s})=t(P(s-1)(u\otimes f^{s})).

Let λ∈K\lambda\in K be a constant. Then specializing the parameter ss to λ\lambda, we obtain left DXD_{X}-modules

ℒ⁡(λ):=ℒ/(s−λ)​ℒ,M⁡(u,f,λ):=M⁡(u,f,s)/(s−λ)​M​(u,f,s).{\mathcal{L}}(\lambda):={\mathcal{L}}/(s-\lambda){\mathcal{L}},\qquad M(u,f,\lambda):=M(u,f,s)/(s-\lambda)M(u,f,s).

Let us denote by fs|s=λf^{s}|_{s=\lambda} and (u⊗fs)|s=λ(u\otimes f^{s})|_{s=\lambda} the residue class of fsf^{s} in ℒ⁡(λ){\mathcal{L}}(\lambda), and that of u⊗fsu\otimes f^{s} in M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda) respectively. Note that M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda) is not, at least a priori, a submodule of M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ⁡(λ)M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}(\lambda). Kashiwara also proved the following fundamental fact, to which we shall give an elementary proof in Section 4.

Theorem 1.3 (Kashiwara [7])

If MM is holonomic on XfX_{f}, then M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda) is a holonomic DXD_{X}-module for any λ∈K\lambda\in K.

On the other hand, the free K⁡[x,f−1]K[x,f^{-1}]-module K⁡[x,f−1]​fλK[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda} with a free generator fλf^{\lambda} has a natural structure of left DXD_{X}-module induced by

∂xi(a⁡(x)​f−k​fλ)=(∂a⁡(x)∂xi​f−k+(λ−k)​fi​a​(x)​f−k−1)​fλ(1≤i≤n)\partial_{x_{i}}(a(x)f^{-k}f^{\lambda})=\left(\frac{\partial a(x)}{\partial x_{i}}f^{-k}+(\lambda-k)f_{i}a(x)f^{-k-1}\right)f^{\lambda}\qquad(1\leq i\leq n)

for a⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]a(x)\in K[x] and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. In particular, this module is isomorphic to the localization M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] if λ\lambda is an integer. We remark that K⁡[x,f−1]​fλK[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda} is not isomorphic to ℒ⁡(λ){\mathcal{L}}(\lambda) in general. For example, set n=1n=1, f=x=x1f=x=x_{1}, and λ=0\lambda=0. Then xs|s=0x^{s}|_{s=0} satisfies x​∂x(xs|s=0)=0x\partial_{x}(x^{s}|_{s=0})=0 but ∂x(xs|s=0)≠0\partial_{x}(x^{s}|_{s=0})\neq 0, while ∂xx0=0\partial_{x}x^{0}=0 by the definition.

Let us define the specialization homomorphism

ρλ:M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ⟶M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλ\rho_{\lambda}:M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}\longrightarrow M\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda}

by

for v∈Mv\in M, a⁡(x,s)∈K⁡[x,s]a(x,s)\in K[x,s], and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. Then ρλ​(P⁡(s)​w)=P⁡(λ)​ρλ​(w)\rho_{\lambda}(P(s)w)=P(\lambda)\rho_{\lambda}(w) holds for any w∈M⊗K⁡[x]ℒw\in M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}} and P​(s)∈DX​[s]P(s)\in D_{X}[s]. Since any element of (s−λ)​M​(u,f,s)(s-\lambda)M(u,f,s) is sent by ρλ\rho_{\lambda} to zero, ρλ\rho_{\lambda} induces a surjective DXD_{X}-homomorphism

ρ~λ:M⁡(u,f,λ)⟶DX​(u⊗fλ)⊂M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλ.\tilde{\rho}_{\lambda}:M(u,f,\lambda)\longrightarrow D_{X}(u\otimes f^{\lambda})\subset M\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda}.
Lemma 1.4

Let M=DX​uM=D_{X}u be a left DXD_{X}-module generated by uu.

  1. (1)

    Every element of M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}} can be expressed as Q​(s)​(u⊗fs−k)Q(s)(u\otimes f^{s-k}) with some Q​(s)∈DX​[s]Q(s)\in D_{X}[s] and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}.

  2. (2)

    Let λ\lambda be an arbitrary element of KK. Then every element of M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλM\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda} can be expressed as Q⁡(u⊗fλ−k)Q(u\otimes f^{\lambda-k}) with some Q∈DXQ\in D_{X} and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}.

Proof: From the identity ∂xi(v⊗fs−k)=(∂xiv)⊗fs−k+v⊗(s−k)​fi​fs−k−1\partial_{x_{i}}(v\otimes f^{s-k})=(\partial_{x_{i}}v)\otimes f^{s-k}+v\otimes(s-k)f_{i}f^{s-k-1} for any v∈Mv\in M and k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}, we get

(∂xiv)⊗fs−k=(∂xif−(s−k)​fi)​(v⊗fs−k−1).(\partial_{x_{i}}v)\otimes f^{s-k}=(\partial_{x_{i}}f-(s-k)f_{i})(v\otimes f^{s-k-1}).

By induction, we can show that for any multi-index α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}, there exists Qα​(s)∈DX​[s]Q_{\alpha}(s)\in D_{X}[s] such that

(∂xαv)⊗fs−k=Qα​(s)​(v⊗fs−k−|α|).(\partial_{x}^{\alpha}v)\otimes f^{s-k}=Q_{\alpha}(s)(v\otimes f^{s-k-|\alpha|}).

This proves the statement (1). The statement (2) can be proved similarly. □\Box

The following proposition should be well-known; see, e.g., Propositions 7.1 and 7.4 of [10]. The case M=K⁡[x]M=K[x] and f=1f=1 was first proved by Kashiwara [6].

Proposition 1.5

Let MM be a left DXD_{X}-module generated by u∈Mu\in M and assume that there exists the bb-function bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s). Let λ\lambda be an element of KK and suppose that bu,f​(λ−k)≠0b_{u,f}(\lambda-k)\neq 0 for any positive integer kk. Then

  1. (1)

    The image ρλ​(M⁡(u,f,s))=DX​(u⊗fλ)\rho_{\lambda}(M(u,f,s))=D_{X}(u\otimes f^{\lambda}) coincides with M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλM\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda}. In other words, M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλM\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda} is generated by u⊗fλu\otimes f^{\lambda} over DXD_{X}.

  2. (2)

    ker⁡ρλ∩M⁡(u,f,s)\ker\rho_{\lambda}\cap M(u,f,s) coincides with (s−λ)​M​(u,f,s)(s-\lambda)M(u,f,s). Hence ρ~λ:M⁡(u,f,λ)→DX​(u⊗fλ)\tilde{\rho}_{\lambda}:M(u,f,\lambda)\rightarrow D_{X}(u\otimes f^{\lambda}) is an isomorphism of left DXD_{X}-modules.

Proof: (1) In view of Lemma 1.4, we have only to show that u⊗fλ−ku\otimes f^{\lambda-k} belongs to ρλ​(M⁡(u,f,s))\rho_{\lambda}(M(u,f,s)) for any k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. This is obvious for k=0k=0 since ρλ​(u⊗fs)=u⊗fλ\rho_{\lambda}(u\otimes f^{s})=u\otimes f^{\lambda}.

Let us show that u⊗fλ−ku\otimes f^{\lambda-k} belongs to ρλ​(M⁡(u,f,s))\rho_{\lambda}(M(u,f,s)). Suppose k≥1k\geq 1. There exists P​(s)∈DX​[s]P(s)\in D_{X}[s] such that P⁡(s)​(u⊗fs+1)=bu,f​(s)​(u⊗fs)P(s)(u\otimes f^{s+1})=b_{u,f}(s)(u\otimes f^{s}). Applying t−kt^{-k}, we get

P⁡(s−k)​(u⊗fs+1−k)=bu,f​(s−k)​(u⊗fs−k)P(s-k)(u\otimes f^{s+1-k})=b_{u,f}(s-k)(u\otimes f^{s-k})

in M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}. Proceeding inductively, we see that there exists P~​(s)∈DX​[s]\tilde{P}(s)\in D_{X}[s] such that

P~(s)(u⊗fs)=bu,f(s−1)⋯bu,f(s−k)u⊗fs−k\tilde{P}(s)(u\otimes f^{s})=b_{u,f}(s-1)\cdots b_{u,f}(s-k)u\otimes f^{s-k} (1)

holds in M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}. The homomorphism ρλ\rho_{\lambda} gives an identity

P~(λ)(u⊗fλ)=bu,f(λ−1)⋯bu,f(λ−k)u⊗fλ−k\tilde{P}(\lambda)(u\otimes f^{\lambda})=b_{u,f}(\lambda-1)\cdots b_{u,f}(\lambda-k)u\otimes f^{\lambda-k}

in M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλM\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda}. Since bu,f​(λ−j)≠0b_{u,f}(\lambda-j)\neq 0 for j=1,…,kj=1,\dots,k by the assumption, it follows that

u⊗fλ−k=1bu,f(λ−1)⋯bu,f(λ−k)​P~​(λ)​(u⊗fλ).u\otimes f^{\lambda-k}=\frac{1}{b_{u,f}(\lambda-1)\cdots b_{u,f}(\lambda-k)}\tilde{P}(\lambda)(u\otimes f^{\lambda}).

The right-hand side belongs to ρλ​(M⁡(u,f,s))\rho_{\lambda}(M(u,f,s)). This completes the proof of (1).

(2) Assume ρλ​(Q⁡(s)​(u⊗fs))=0\rho_{\lambda}(Q(s)(u\otimes f^{s}))=0 with Q​(s)∈DX​[s]Q(s)\in D_{X}[s]. There exist l∈ℕl\in{\mathbb{N}} and Qj∈DXQ_{j}\in D_{X} which are zero except finitely many indices jj such that

Let us recall local cohomology of DD-modules. Let MM be a finitely generated left DXD_{X}-module, and II be an ideal of K⁡[x]K[x]. Then the kk-th local cohomology group HIk​(M)H^{k}_{I}(M) supported by II is defined to be the kk-th derived functor of the functor

M⟼HI0​(M)={u∈M∣Ik​u=0​ for some k∈ℕ}.M\longmapsto H^{0}_{I}(M)=\{u\in M\mid I^{k}u=0\mbox{ for some $k\in{\mathbb{N}}$}\}.

They have natural structure of left DXD_{X}-module, and they are holonomic if so is MM as was proved by Kashiwara in the analytic category [7].

If II is the principal ideal (f)(f) generated by f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x], then there exists an exact sequence

0⟶H(f)0​(M)⟶M⟶ιM⁡[f−1]⟶H(f)1​(M)→00\longrightarrow H^{0}_{(f)}(M)\longrightarrow M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\iota}}{{\longrightarrow}}M[f^{-1}]\longrightarrow H^{1}_{(f)}(M)\rightarrow 0

of left DXD_{X}-modules, where ι\iota stands for the natural homomorphism such that ι⁡(v)=v⊗1\iota(v)=v\otimes 1 in M⁡[f−1]=M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]M[f^{-1}]=M\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}] for v∈Mv\in M. Hence there is an isomorphism H(f)1​(M)≅M⁡[f−1]/ι⁡(M)H^{1}_{(f)}(M)\cong M[f^{-1}]/\iota(M) as left DXD_{X}-module.

In general, algorithms to compute HIi​(M)H^{i}_{I}(M) as left DXD_{X}-module were given in [10] for the case II is principal, and in [18] and [13] for general II, under the condition that MM is holonomic.

Henece M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] is generated by u⊗f−ku\otimes f^{-k}. □\Box

both of which are not holonomic.

3 Algorithm for M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) and the bb-function

The purpose here is to give algorithms to compute M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s), M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda), M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]​fλM\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}]f^{\lambda}, and the bb-function bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) for an arbitrary DXD_{X}-module M=DX​uM=D_{X}u that is holonomic on XfX_{f}, and an arbitrary non-constant polynomial ff. Algorithms for these objects were already given in [10] under the additional assumption that MM is ff-saturated. We remove this assumption by using the localization algorithm.

Set X=KnX=K^{n} and Y=Kn+1Y=K^{n+1} with coordinates x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) of XX and (x,t)(x,t) of YY. Let f=f⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]f=f(x)\in K[x] be a non-constant polynomial and let ZZ be the affine subset Z={(x,t)∣t=f⁡(x)}Z=\{(x,t)\mid t=f(x)\} of YY. (Note that ZZ is different from what was defined in the previous section.) We regard the local cohomology group

BZ|Y:=HZ1​(K⁡[x,t])=K⁡[x,t,(t−f)−1]/K⁡[x,t]B_{Z|Y}:=H^{1}_{Z}(K[x,t])=K[x,t,(t-f)^{-1}]/K[x,t]

as a left DYD_{Y}-module. For k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, let

δ(k)​(t−f⁡(x))=[(−1)k​k!(t−f⁡(x))k+1]\delta^{(k)}(t-f(x))=\left[\frac{(-1)^{k}k!}{(t-f(x))^{k+1}}\right]

be the residue class in BZ|XB_{Z|X} and denote δ⁡(t−f)=δ(0)​(t−f)\delta(t-f)=\delta^{(0)}(t-f). Then δ⁡(t−f)\delta(t-f) satisfies a holonomic system

(t−f)δ(t−f)=(∂xi+fi∂t)δ(t−f)=0(1≤i≤n)(t-f)\delta(t-f)=(\partial_{x_{i}}+f_{i}\partial_{t})\delta(t-f)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq n)

with fi=∂f/∂xif_{i}=\partial f/\partial x_{i}. Hence there exists an isomorphism

BZ|Y≅DY/(DY(t−f)+DY(∂x1+f1∂t)+⋯+DY(∂xn+fn∂t))B_{Z|Y}\cong D_{Y}/(D_{Y}(t-f)+D_{Y}(\partial_{x_{1}}+f_{1}\partial_{t})+\cdots+D_{Y}(\partial_{x_{n}}+f_{n}\partial_{t}))

as left DYD_{Y}-modules. In particular, δ(k)​(t−f)\delta^{(k)}(t-f) (k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}) constitute a free basis of BZ|YB_{Z|Y} over K⁡[x]K[x].

Following B. Malgrange, let us give ℒ=DX​[s]​fs{\mathcal{L}}=D_{X}[s]f^{s} a structure of left DYD_{Y}-module by

t⁡(a⁡(x,s)​f−k​fs)=a⁡(x,s+1)​f−k+1​fs,∂t(a⁡(x,s)​f−k​fs)=−s​a​(x,s−1)​f−k−1​fst(a(x,s)f^{-k}f^{s})=a(x,s+1)f^{-k+1}f^{s},\qquad\partial_{t}(a(x,s)f^{-k}f^{s})=-sa(x,s-1)f^{-k-1}f^{s}

for a⁡(x,s)∈K⁡[x,s]a(x,s)\in K[x,s] and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. The actions of tt and ∂t\partial_{t} on ℒ{\mathcal{L}} satisfy [∂t,t]=1[\partial_{t},t]=1, and they commute with xix_{i}, ∂xi\partial_{x_{i}}. Hence the definition above extends to the action of DYD_{Y} on ℒ{\mathcal{L}}. In particular, ∂tt​fs=−s​fs\partial_{t}tf^{s}=-sf^{s} holds, which will play an important role in what follows.

With respect to this action, BZ|YB_{Z|Y} can be regarded as a left DYD_{Y}-submodule of ℒ{\mathcal{L}} by identifying δ(k)​(t−f)\delta^{(k)}(t-f) with (−1)ks(s−1)⋯(s−k+1)fs−k(-1)^{k}s(s-1)\cdots(s-k+1)f^{s-k} in ℒ{\mathcal{L}}. In fact, we have

t​δ(k)​(t−f)=f​δ(k)​(t−f)−k​δ(k−1)​(t−f),\displaystyle t\delta^{(k)}(t-f)=f\delta^{(k)}(t-f)-k\delta^{(k-1)}(t-f),

=f(−1)ks(s−1)⋯(s−k+1)fs−k−(−1)k−1ks(s−1)⋯(s−k+2)fs−k+1\displaystyle=f(-1)^{k}s(s-1)\cdots(s-k+1)f^{s-k}-(-1)^{k-1}ks(s-1)\cdots(s-k+2)f^{s-k+1}

since (t−f)​δ(k)​(t−f)=−k​δ(k−1)​(t−f)(t-f)\delta^{(k)}(t-f)=-k\delta^{(k-1)}(t-f), and

∂tδ(k)​(t−f)=δ(k+1)​(t−f),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\delta^{(k)}(t-f)=\delta^{(k+1)}(t-f),
∂t((−1)ks(s−1)⋯(s−k+1)fs−k)=(−1)k+1s(s−1)⋯(s−k)fs−k−1.\displaystyle\partial_{t}((-1)^{k}s(s-1)\cdots(s-k+1)f^{s-k})=(-1)^{k+1}s(s-1)\cdots(s-k)f^{s-k-1}.

For a left DXD_{X}-module M=DX​uM=D_{X}u, consider the tensor product M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|YM\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y}, which is a left DYD_{Y}-module.

Definition 3.1

Set ϑ′i:=∂xi+fi∂t\vartheta^{\prime}_{i}:=\partial_{x_{i}}+f_{i}\partial_{t} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Define a ring homomorphism τ′\tau^{\prime} from DXD_{X} to DYD_{Y} by

τ′:DX∋P(x,∂x)⟼P(x,ϑ1′,…,ϑn′)∈DY.\tau^{\prime}:D_{X}\ni P(x,\partial_{x})\longmapsto P(x,\vartheta^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\vartheta^{\prime}_{n})\in D_{Y}.

Since ϑ1′,…,ϑn′\vartheta^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\vartheta^{\prime}_{n} commute with each other, and [ϑi′,xj]=δi​j[\vartheta^{\prime}_{i},x_{j}]=\delta_{ij}, this substitution is a well-defined ring homomorphism.

Since ϑi′​δ​(t−f)=0\vartheta^{\prime}_{i}\delta(t-f)=0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

τ′​(P)​(v⊗δ⁡(t−f))=P​v⊗δ⁡(t−f)\tau^{\prime}(P)(v\otimes\delta(t-f))=Pv\otimes\delta(t-f)

holds for any v∈Mv\in M and P∈DXP\in D_{X}. Hence we have

P​u⊗∂tkδ⁡(t−f)=∂tk(P​u⊗δ⁡(t−f))=∂tkτ′​(P)​(u⊗δ⁡(t−f)).Pu\otimes\partial_{t}^{k}\delta(t-f)=\partial_{t}^{k}(Pu\otimes\delta(t-f))=\partial_{t}^{k}\tau^{\prime}(P)(u\otimes\delta(t-f)).

This proves

Lemma 3.2

If M=DX​uM=D_{X}u, then the left DYD_{Y}-module M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|YM\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y} is generated by u⊗δ⁡(t−f)u\otimes\delta(t-f).

Theorem 3.3

Let M=DX​uM=D_{X}u be a left DXD_{X}-module generated by uu and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x]. Let GG be a finite set of generators of I:=AnnDX​uI:={\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{X}}u and let JJ be the left ideal of DYD_{Y} generated by {τ′​(P)∣P∈G}∪{t−f}\{\tau^{\prime}(P)\mid P\in G\}\cup\{t-f\}. Then JJ coincides with the annihilator AnnDY​(u⊗δ⁡(t−f)){\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{Y}}(u\otimes\delta(t-f)). Moreover, if MM is a holonomic DXD_{X}-module, then M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|YM\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y} is a holonomic DYD_{Y}-module.

The first part of this proposition was proved by Walther [18]. The proof is almost the same as the proof of Theorem 2.11. The last assertion can be proved in the same way as Theorem 2.14.

Thus we have an algorithm to compute M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|YM\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y}, which was already given in [10]. The inclusion BZ|X⊂ℒB_{Z|X}\subset{\mathcal{L}} induces a homomorphism

ψ:M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|Y⟶M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ\psi:M\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y}\longrightarrow M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}

of left DYD_{Y}-modules. The image of ψ\psi coincides with M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s).

Our main aim is to compute the DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-submodule M⁡(u,f,s)=DX​[s]​(u⊗fs)M(u,f,s)=D_{X}[s](u\otimes f^{s}) of M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}. The following lemma was proved in [10] as Proposition 6.13.

Lemma 3.4

The homomorphism ψ\psi above is injective if and only if H(f)0​(M)=0H_{(f)}^{0}(M)=0; i.e., MM is ff-saturated,

Proof: An arbitrary element of M⊗K⁡[x]BZ|YM\otimes_{K[x]}B_{Z|Y} is expressed uniquely as

w=∑j=0kvj⊗δ(j)​(t−f)w=\sum_{j=0}^{k}v_{j}\otimes\delta^{(j)}(t-f)

with k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} and vj∈Mv_{j}\in M. Then

ψ(w)=∑j=0k(−1)jvj⊗(s(s−1)⋯(s−j+1)f−jfs)\psi(w)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}v_{j}\otimes(s(s-1)\cdots(s-j+1)f^{-j}f^{s})

vanishes if and only if each vj⊗f−jv_{j}\otimes f^{-j} vanishes in M⊗K⁡[x]K⁡[x,f−1]M\otimes_{K[x]}K[x,f^{-1}], which is equivalent to vj∈H(f)0​(M)v_{j}\in H^{0}_{(f)}(M). □\Box

Lemma 3.5

Let M=DX​uM=D_{X}u be a left DXD_{X}-module generated by uu and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] be a non-constant polynomial. Let ι:M→M⁡[f−1]\iota:M\rightarrow M[f^{-1}] be the canonical homomorphsm. Then ι\iota induces isomorphisms

M⊗K⁡[x]ℒ⟶∼ι⁡(M)⊗K⁡[x]ℒ,M⁡(u,f,s)⟶∼ι⁡(M)​(u,f,s)M\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\iota(M)\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}},\qquad M(u,f,s)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\iota(M)(u,f,s)

of left DX​[s]D_{X}[s]-modules.

Proof: Since ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is isomorphic to K⁡[x,f−1,s]K[x,f^{-1},s] as a K⁡[x,s]K[x,s]-module, we have only to show that the natural homomorphism M⁡[f−1]→ι⁡(M)​[f−1]M[f^{-1}]\rightarrow\iota(M)[f^{-1}] is an isomorphism. For any v∈Mv\in M, v⊗1=0v\otimes 1=0 holds in M⁡[f−1]M[f^{-1}] if and only if fk​v=0f^{k}v=0 in MM with some k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. This is equivalent to ι⁡(v)⊗1=0\iota(v)\otimes 1=0 in ι​(M)​[f−1]\iota(M)[f^{-1}]. Hence the first homomorphism is an isomorphism. This implies the injectivity of the second homomorphism, the surjectivity of which is obvious by the definition. □\Box

Algorithm 3.6 (Computing M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) and M⁡(u,f,λ)M(u,f,\lambda))

Input: M=DX​u=DX/IM=D_{X}u=D_{X}/I with a finite set of generators of II, a non-constant f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x], and λ∈K\lambda\in K.

    Compute ι⁡(M)=DX/AnnDY​ι​(u)\iota(M)=D_{X}/{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{Y}}\iota(u) by the localization algorithm.

    Compute J=AnnDY​(ι⁡(u)⊗δ⁡(t−f))J={\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{Y}}(\iota(u)\otimes\delta(t-f)) by using Theorem 3.3.

    Compute J∩DX​[s]J\cap D_{X}[s], which is equal to AnnDX​[s]​(u⊗fs){\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{X}[s]}(u\otimes f^{s}).

    The substitution s=λs=\lambda for generators of J∩DX​[s]J\cap D_{X}[s] gives a set of generators of AnnDX​(u⊗fs)|s=λ{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{X}}(u\otimes f^{s})|_{s=\lambda}.

Proposition 3.7

Let M=DX​uM=D_{X}u be a left DXD_{X}-module generated by uu and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] a non-constant polynomial. Then the bb-function bu,f​(x)b_{u,f}(x) exists if and only if there exists a nonzero polynomial b⁡(s)∈K⁡[s]b(s)\in K[s] such that

b(−∂tt)(u⊗δ(t−f))∈tDX[t∂t](u⊗δ(t−f))=DX[t∂t]t(u⊗δ(t−f))=DX[t∂t]f(u⊗δ(t−f)).b(-\partial_{t}t)(u\otimes\delta(t-f))\in tD_{X}[t\partial_{t}](u\otimes\delta(t-f))=D_{X}[t\partial_{t}]t(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=D_{X}[t\partial_{t}]f(u\otimes\delta(t-f)). (2)

If MM is ff-saturated and such b⁡(s)b(s) exists, then bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) is the monic polynomial of the minimum degree among such b⁡(s)b(s).

Proof: Assume that (2) holds. Then there exists P​(s)∈DX​[s]P(s)\in D_{X}[s] such that

b(−∂tt)(u⊗δ(t−f))=P(−∂tt)f(u⊗δ(t−f)).b(-\partial_{t}t)(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=P(-\partial_{t}t)f(u\otimes\delta(t-f)).

Applying the homomorphism ψ\psi we get b⁡(s)​(u⊗fs)=P⁡(s)​(u⊗fs+1)b(s)(u\otimes f^{s})=P(s)(u\otimes f^{s+1}). Hence bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) exists and divides b⁡(s)b(s).

On the other hand, assume that there exist nonzero b⁡(s)∈K⁡[s]b(s)\in K[s] and P​(s)∈DX​[s]P(s)\in D_{X}[s] such that b⁡(s)​(u⊗fs)=P⁡(s)​(u⊗fs+1)b(s)(u\otimes f^{s})=P(s)(u\otimes f^{s+1}) holds in M⊗K⁡[x]ℒM\otimes_{K[x]}{\mathcal{L}}. Then as is seen by the proof of Lemma 3.4, there exists k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} such that

fkb(−∂tt)(u⊗δ(t−f))=fkP(−∂tt)f(u⊗δ(t−f)).f^{k}b(-\partial_{t}t)(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=f^{k}P(-\partial_{t}t)f(u\otimes\delta(t-f)).

Since

fkb(−∂tt)(u⊗δ(t−f))=b(−∂tt)fk(u⊗δ(t−f))=b(−∂tt)tk(u⊗δ(t−f))f^{k}b(-\partial_{t}t)(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=b(-\partial_{t}t)f^{k}(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=b(-\partial_{t}t)t^{k}(u\otimes\delta(t-f))

holds, we get

∂tkb(−∂tt)tk(u⊗δ(t−f))=∂tkfkP(−∂tt)f(u⊗δ(t−f))∈DX[t∂t]f(u⊗δ(t−f)).\partial_{t}^{k}b(-\partial_{t}t)t^{k}(u\otimes\delta(t-f))=\partial_{t}^{k}f^{k}P(-\partial_{t}t)f(u\otimes\delta(t-f))\in D_{X}[t\partial_{t}]f(u\otimes\delta(t-f)).

This completes the proof because there exists c⁡(s)∈K⁡[x]c(s)\in K[x] such that ∂tkb(−∂tt)tk=c(−∂tt)\partial_{t}^{k}b(-\partial_{t}t)t^{k}=c(-\partial_{t}t). □\Box

Now we obtain an algorithm to determine whether the bb-function exists and to compute it if it does:

Algorithm 3.8 (Computing the bb-function bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s))


Input: M=DX​u=DX/IM=D_{X}u=D_{X}/I with a finite set of generators of II and a non-constant f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x].

Output: the bb-function bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) if it exists. ‘No’ if it does not exist.

  1. (1)

    Compute a set of generators of J:=AnnDX​[s]​(u⊗fs)J:={\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{X}[s]}(u\otimes f^{s}) by the preceding algorithm.

    Compute I⁡(u,f)=(J+DX​[s]​f)∩K⁡[s]I(u,f)=(J+D_{X}[s]f)\cap K[s] by elimination. The monic generator of I⁡(u,f)I(u,f) is bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s).

    Compute M⁡(u,f,s)M(u,f,s) and bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) by preceding algorithms. Quit if bu,f​(s)b_{u,f}(s) does not exist.

    Let k0k_{0} be the maximum nonzero integer, if any, such that bu,f​(λ−k0)=0b_{u,f}(\lambda-k_{0})=0. If there is no such k0k_{0}, then set k0=0k_{0}=0.

4 Length and multiplicity of DD-modules

W set X=KnX=K^{n} as in the preceding sections. First let us recall basic facts about the length and the multiplicity of a left DXD_{X}-module following J. Bernstein ([1],[2]). Let MM be a finitely generated left DXD_{X}-module. A composition series of MM of length kk is a sequence

M=M0⊃M1⊃⋯⊃Mk=0M=M_{0}\supset M_{1}\supset\cdots\supset M_{k}=0

of left DnD_{n}-submodules such that Mi/Mi−1M_{i}/M_{i-1} is a nonzero simple left DXD_{X}-module (i.e. having no proper left DXD_{X}-submodule other than 00) for i=1,…​ki=1,\dots k. The length of MM, which we denote by length​M{\mathrm{length}\,}M, is the least length of composition series (if any) of MM. If there is no composition series, the length of MM is defined to be infinite. The length is additive in the sense that if

0⟶N⟶M⟶L⟶00\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0

is an exact sequence of left DXD_{X}-modules of finite length, then length​M=length​N+length​L{\mathrm{length}\,}M={\mathrm{length}\,}N+{\mathrm{length}\,}L holds.

For each integer kk, set

Fk(DX)={∑|α|+|β|≤kaα​βxα∂β∣aα​β∈K}}.F_{k}(D_{X})=\Bigl\{\sum_{|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq k}a_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\mid a_{\alpha\beta}\in K\}\Bigr\}.

In particular, we have Fk​(DX)=0F_{k}(D_{X})=0 for k<0k<0 and F0​(DX)=KF_{0}(D_{X})=K. The filtration {Fk​(DX)}k∈ℤ\{F_{k}(D_{X})\}_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}} is called the Bernstein filtration on DXD_{X}.

Let MM be a finitely generated left DXD_{X}-module. A family {Fk​(M)}k∈ℤ\{F_{k}(M)\}_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}} of KK-subspaces of MM is called a Bernstein filtration on MM if it satisfies

  1. (1)

    Fk​(M)⊂Fk+1​(M)(∀k∈ℤ),⋃k∈ℤFk​(M)=MF_{k}(M)\subset F_{k+1}(M)\quad(\forall k\in{\mathbb{Z}}),\qquad\bigcup_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}F_{k}(M)=M

  2. (2)

    Fj​(DX)​Fk​(M)⊂Fj+k​(M)(∀j,k∈ℤ)F_{j}(D_{X})F_{k}(M)\subset F_{j+k}(M)\quad(\forall j,k\in{\mathbb{Z}})

Moreover, {Fk​(M)}\{F_{k}(M)\} is called a good Bernstein filtration if there exist ui∈Fki​(M)u_{i}\in F_{k_{i}}(M) (i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m) such that

Fk​(M)=Fk−k1​(DX)​u1+⋯+Fk−km​(DX)​um(∀k∈ℤ).F_{k}(M)=F_{k-k_{1}}(D_{X})u_{1}+\cdots+F_{k-k_{m}}(D_{X})u_{m}\qquad(\forall k\in{\mathbb{Z}}).

If {Fk​(M)}\{F_{k}(M)\} is a good Bernstein filtration, then each Fk​(M)F_{k}(M) is a finite dimensional vector space over KK and Fk​(M)=0F_{k}(M)=0 for k≪0k\ll 0 (see e.g., 1.3 of [11]).

Let {Fk​(M)}\{F_{k}(M)\} be a good Bernstein filtration on MM. Then there exists a polynomial p⁡(T)=cd​Td+cd−1​Td−1+⋯+c0∈ℚ⁡[T]p(T)=c_{d}T^{d}+c_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{0}\in{\mathbb{Q}}[T] such that

dimKFk​(M)=p⁡(k)(k≫0)\dim_{K}F_{k}(M)=p(k)\quad(k\gg 0)

and d!​cdd!c_{d} is a positive integer. We call p⁡(T)p(T) the Hilbert polynomial of MM with respect to the filtration {Fk​(M)}\{F_{k}(M)\}. The leading term of p⁡(T)p(T) does not depend on the choice of a good Bernstein filtration {Fk​(M)}\{F_{k}(M)\}. The degree dd of the Hilbert polynomial p⁡(T)p(T) is called the dimension of MM and denoted dimM\dim M. The multiplicity of MM, denoted mult​M{\mathrm{mult}\,}M is defined to be the positive integer d!​cdd!c_{d}. The dimension and the multiplicity are invariants of a finitely generated left DXD_{X}-module.

If M≠0M\neq 0, then the dimension of MM is not less than nn (Bernstein’s inequality). By definition, MM is holonomic if M=0M=0 or dimM=n\dim M=n. If MM is a holonomic left DXD_{X}-module, we have an inequality length​M≤mult​M{\mathrm{length}\,}M\leq{\mathrm{mult}\,}M and hence MM is of finite length in particular. Moreover, the multiplicity is additive for holonomic left DXD_{X}-modules.

We can compute the dimension and the multiplicity of a given finitely generated (not necessarily holonomic) DXD_{X}-module by using a Gröbner basis with respect to a term order compatible with the Bernstein filtration.

Example 4.1

Let MM be the DXD_{X}-module with X=K2X=K^{2} defined in Example 3.11. We get exact sequences

with H(f)0​(M)≅H(x,y)2​(K⁡[x,y])≅H(f)1​(M)H^{0}_{(f)}(M)\cong H^{2}_{(x,y)}(K[x,y])\cong H^{1}_{(f)}(M). We have

mult​M=mult​M​[f−1]=6,mult​ι​(M)=5,mult​H(f)0​(M)=mult​H(f)1​(M)=1.{\mathrm{mult}\,}M={\mathrm{mult}\,}M[f^{-1}]=6,\quad{\mathrm{mult}\,}\iota(M)=5,\quad{\mathrm{mult}\,}H^{0}_{(f)}(M)={\mathrm{mult}\,}H^{1}_{(f)}(M)=1.

The following two propositions are easy and should be well-known.

Proposition 4.2

Let f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] be a non-constant polynomial. Then the multiplicity of the left DXD_{X}-module K⁡[x,f−1]K[x,f^{-1}] is at most (deg⁡f+1)n(\deg f+1)^{n}.

Proof: Let dd be the degree of ff.

Fk(K[x,f−1]):={afk+1∣a∈K[x1,…,xn],dega≤(d+1)k}(k∈ℤ),F_{k}(K[x,f^{-1}]):=\left\{\frac{a}{f^{k+1}}\mid a\in K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],\,\deg a\leq(d+1)k\right\}\quad(k\in{\mathbb{Z}}),

is a (not necessarily good) Bernstein filtration on MM with

dimKFk​(K⁡[x,f−1])=(n+(d+1)​kn).\dim_{K}F_{k}(K[x,f^{-1}])=\binom{n+(d+1)k}{n}.

This implies dimK⁡[x,f−1]=n\dim K[x,f^{-1}]=n and mult​M≤(d+1)n{\mathrm{mult}\,}M\leq(d+1)^{n}. □\Box

Let n=1n=1 and f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1}] be non-constant square free. Then one has mult​K​[x,f−1]=deg⁡f+1\,\,{\mathrm{mult}\,}K[x,f^{-1}]=\deg f+1.

dimFk​(M)\displaystyle\dim F_{k}(M) =dimFk​(D1)−dimFk−d​(D1)\displaystyle=\dim F_{k}(D_{1})-\dim F_{k-d}(D_{1})
=(k+22)−(k−d+22)=d​k−12​(d−1)​(d−2),\displaystyle=\binom{k+2}{2}-\binom{k-d+2}{2}=dk-\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(d-2),

hods for k≥dk\geq d, the multiplicity of MM is dd. □\Box

We conjecture that the multiplicity of MA​(β1,β2)M_{A}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) is 1616 for all (β1,β2)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) except (1,2)(1,2), as is the case with the holonomic rank (see [15]).
